Stoichiometry.explanation: From the stoichiometric ratio: $3\text{ volumes of } \text{H}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{ volumes of } \text{NH}_3$. Volume of $\text{NH}_3 = 6.0 \times (2/3) = 4.0\text{ dm}^3$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Total Number of Atoms in Molecule
Stoichiometry.question: How many total atoms are present in one formula unit of Aluminium Sulfate ($\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$)?
Stoichiometry.explanation: In $\text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3$: $2\text{ atoms of Al} + 3(1\text{ atom of S} + 4\text{ atoms of O}) = 2 + 3 + 12 = 17\text{ total atoms}$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: What is the Molar Mass of Sulfuric Acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$)? (Given atomic masses: $\text{H}=1.01, \text{S}=32.07, \text{O}=16.00$)

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: If $0.20\text{ moles}$ of Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$) are dissolved in water to make a total solution volume of $500\text{ cm}^3$ ($0.50\text{ dm}^3$), what is the Molarity of the solution?
Stoichiometry.explanation: $\text{Molarity } (M) = \text{moles of solute} / \text{volume in } \text{dm}^3 = 0.20\text{ mol} / 0.50\text{ dm}^3 = 0.40\text{ M}$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: How many grams of Oxygen ($\text{O}_2$) are required for the complete combustion of $16.0\text{ g}$ of Methane ($\text{CH}_4$)? Reaction: $\text{CH}_4 + 2\text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$ (Atomic masses: $\text{C}=12, \text{H}=1, \text{O}=16$)
Stoichiometry.explanation: $16.0\text{ g } \text{CH}_4 = 1.0\text{ mol } \text{CH}_4$. Stoichiometry requires $2.0\text{ mol } \text{O}_2 = 2.0 \times 32.0\text{ g/mol} = 64.0\text{ g } \text{O}_2$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: By international IUPAC agreement, the unified atomic mass unit ($1\text{ amu}$ / Dalton) is defined precisely as:

options.A: Exactly $\frac{1}{12}\text{th}$ the mass of a single unbound ground-state Carbon-12 ($^{12}_6\text{C}$) atom
options.B: The exact mass of one hydrogen atom
options.C: The mass of one oxygen-16 atom
options.D: The mass of one mole of electrons

Stoichiometry.explanation: $1\text{ amu}$ is defined as $1/12$ of the mass of a Carbon-12 atom, which equals approximately $1.66054 \times 10^{-24}\text{ grams}$ ($1.66054 \times 10^{-27}\text{ kg}$).

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Molar Mass Calculation of Hydrated Copper Sulfate
Stoichiometry.question: What is the formula mass of Hydrated Copper(II) Sulfate crystals ($\text{CuSO}_4 \cdot 5\text{H}_2\text{O}$)? (Atomic masses: $\text{Cu}=63.5, \text{S}=32, \text{O}=16, \text{H}=1$)

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Molar Volume at Standard Ambient Temperature and Pressure (SATP)
Stoichiometry.question: While 1 mole of any ideal gas occupies $22.4\text{ dm}^3$ at STP ($0^\circ\text{C}, 1\text{ atm}$), what volume does it occupy at SATP ($25^\circ\text{C}, 1\text{ bar} / 1\text{ atm}$)?
Stoichiometry.explanation: At standard ambient temperature and pressure ($298\text{ K}, 1\text{ atm}$), using $V = nRT/P$, 1 mole of an ideal gas occupies approximately $24.0\text{ dm}^3$ ($24\text{ L}$).

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Theoretical vs Actual Yield and Percentage Yield
Stoichiometry.question: If the theoretical yield of a chemical reaction is calculated to be $50.0\text{ g}$, but the actual mass of purified product isolated in the lab is $42.5\text{ g}$, what is the Percentage Yield?
Stoichiometry.explanation: $\text{Percentage Yield} = (\text{Actual Yield} / \text{Theoretical Yield}) \times 100 = (42.5 / 50.0) \times 100 = 85.0\%$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: In the reaction $2\text{H}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$, if $4\text{ moles of } \text{H}_2$ react with $4\text{ moles of } \text{O}_2$, how many moles of the excess reagent remain unreacted?
Stoichiometry.explanation: Stoichiometry requires $2\text{ moles } \text{H}_2$ per $1\text{ mole } \text{O}_2$. Thus $4\text{ moles } \text{H}_2$ consumes $2\text{ moles } \text{O}_2$. Remaining excess $\text{O}_2 = 4 - 2 = 2\text{ moles}$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: What volume of concentrated $12.0\text{ M } \text{HCl}$ stock solution is required to prepare $600\text{ mL}$ of $0.50\text{ M } \text{HCl}$ solution?
Stoichiometry.explanation: Using dilution formula $M_1 V_1 = M_2 V_2 \rightarrow 12.0 \times V_1 = 0.50 \times 600 \rightarrow V_1 = 300 / 12.0 = 25.0\text{ mL}$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Mass Percentage of Water in Washing Soda
Stoichiometry.question: What is the mass percentage of crystallization water in Washing Soda ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$)? (Molar mass of anhydrous $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 = 106\text{ g/mol}$, $\text{H}_2\text{O} = 18\text{ g/mol}$)
Stoichiometry.explanation: Total molar mass $= 106 + 10(18) = 286\text{ g/mol}$. Mass of water $= 180\text{ g}$. $\%\text{H}_2\text{O} = (180 / 286) \times 100 = 62.93\%$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Volume of CO2 from Calcium Carbonate Thermal Decomposition
Stoichiometry.question: What volume of Carbon Dioxide gas (measured at STP) is liberated by the complete thermal decomposition of $10.0\text{ g}$ of pure Limestone ($\text{CaCO}_3$, molar mass $= 100\text{ g/mol}$)?
Stoichiometry.explanation: $\text{CaCO}_3 \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CaO} + \text{CO}_2$. $10.0\text{ g} / 100 = 0.10\text{ mole } \text{CaCO}_3$, which yields $0.10\text{ mole } \text{CO}_2$. Volume at STP $= 0.10 \times 22.4 = 2.24\text{ dm}^3$.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.topic: Avogadro's Number of Atoms in Molecule
Stoichiometry.question: How many total individual atoms are present in $1\text{ mole}$ of Glucose ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6$)?
Stoichiometry.explanation: One molecule of glucose contains $6 + 12 + 6 = 24$ atoms. Thus 1 mole contains $24 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 1.445 \times 10^{25}$ total atoms.

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: A hydrocarbon compound contains $80\%$ Carbon and $20\%$ Hydrogen by mass. What is its simplest Empirical Formula? (Atomic masses: $\text{C}=12, \text{H}=1$)

Stoichiometry.subject: Chemistry
Stoichiometry.question: If a drinking water sample contains $0.005\text{ g}$ of toxic arsenic dissolved in $1000\text{ g}$ ($1\text{ kg}$) of water, what is the concentration in Parts Per Million ($\text{ppm}$)?
Stoichiometry.explanation: $\text{ppm} = (\text{Mass of solute} / \text{Mass of solution}) \times 10^6 = (0.005 / 1000) \times 10^6 = 5.0\text{ ppm}$ (or $5\text{ mg/L}$).

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In classical and modern redox chemistry, Reduction is defined as the:

options.A: Gain of electrons or decrease in oxidation state
options.B: Loss of electrons or increase in oxidation state

Electrochemistry.explanation: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss of electrons; Reduction Is Gain of electrons (which reduces or lowers the oxidation state).

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: What is the oxidation number of Sulfur in the Sulfate polyatomic anion ($\text{SO}_4^{2-}$)?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Let $S = x$. Oxygen is $-2$. $x + 4(-2) = -2 \Rightarrow x - 8 = -2 \Rightarrow x = +6$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In an operating Galvanic (Voltaic) cell (such as a Daniell cell), what spontaneous energy conversion occurs?

options.A: Spontaneous chemical energy is converted into electrical energy
options.B: Electrical energy is used to drive non-spontaneous chemical reactions
options.C: Nuclear energy is converted into thermal radiation
options.D: Light energy is converted into mechanical work

Electrochemistry.explanation: A galvanic (voltaic) cell utilizes spontaneous chemical redox reactions between electrodes to generate an electric potential and current.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In all electrochemical and electrolytic cells, oxidation always takes place at the:
Electrochemistry.explanation: By convention and definition: Anode is the site of Oxidation (An Ox), and Cathode is the site of Reduction (Red Cat).

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In a standard Daniell cell, Zinc ($\text{Zn}$) acts as the anode while Copper ($\text{Cu}$) acts as the cathode. What is the overall cell reaction?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Zinc is more reactive (higher oxidation potential) and is oxidized to $\text{Zn}^{2+}$, while $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions are reduced to metallic copper at the cathode.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: What is the primary function of a salt bridge containing saturated $\text{KCl}$ or $\text{KNO}_3$ in a voltaic cell?

options.A: To maintain electrical neutrality by allowing ionic migration between half-cells
options.B: To supply metallic electrons directly to the external wire
options.C: To accelerate the rate of electron evaporation into air
options.D: To prevent all chemical reactions from taking place

Electrochemistry.explanation: The salt bridge completes the electrical circuit and maintains electrolytic charge neutrality by allowing anions and cations to diffuse between half-cells.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: During the industrial electrolysis of molten Sodium Chloride in a Downs Cell, what product is liberated at the anode?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Chloride ions ($\text{Cl}^-$) undergo oxidation at the positive carbon anode to produce chlorine gas: $2\text{Cl}^- \rightarrow \text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{e}^-$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: When electroplating a brass spoon with pure Silver ($\text{Ag}$), the spoon must be connected to the:

options.A: Cathode (negative terminal of DC power source)
options.B: Anode (positive terminal of DC power source)

Electrochemistry.explanation: The object to be electroplated is made the cathode so that positive metal cations ($\text{Ag}^+$) are attracted to it and reduced to a uniform metallic coating.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Which of the following environmental combinations is strictly necessary for iron to undergo rusting?

options.C: Pure water completely devoid of dissolved oxygen

Electrochemistry.explanation: Rusting is an electrochemical corrosion process requiring both oxygen and liquid/moist water to form hydrated iron(III) oxide: $4\text{Fe} + 3\text{O}_2 + 2x\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Protecting underground iron pipelines by connecting them to blocks of Zinc or Magnesium is known as:
Electrochemistry.explanation: Zinc and Magnesium are more easily oxidized than iron, serving as sacrificial anodes that corrode preferentially, keeping the iron structure cathodic and uncorroded.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: What is the oxidation state of Chromium in the Potassium Dichromate compound ($\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$)?
Electrochemistry.explanation: $2(+1) + 2(\text{Cr}) + 7(-2) = 0 \Rightarrow 2 + 2\text{Cr} - 14 = 0 \Rightarrow 2\text{Cr} = +12 \Rightarrow \text{Cr} = +6$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.topic: Cathodic Protection of Underground Iron Pipes
Electrochemistry.question: In the cathodic protection (sacrificial anode method) of underground iron steel pipelines, which highly active metal is connected as the sacrificial anode?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Magnesium and Zinc have more negative standard reduction potentials than Iron, meaning they oxidize preferentially ('sacrifice themselves') and protect the steel pipe from corrosion.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In the industrial Down's Cell for extracting metallic sodium by electrolysis of molten $\text{NaCl}$, Calcium Chloride ($\text{CaCl}_2$) is added to the electrolyte to:

options.A: Lower the melting point of $\text{NaCl}$ from $801^\circ\text{C}$ down to approximately $600^\circ\text{C}$
options.B: Increase the density of chlorine gas
options.C: Prevent sodium metal from reacting with air

Electrochemistry.explanation: Adding $\text{CaCl}_2$ forms a eutectic mixture, lowering the operating temperature of molten $\text{NaCl}$ from $801^circ\ext{C}$ to $\sim 600^circ\ext{C}$, saving energy and reducing sodium vaporization.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Based on the electrochemical series, what happens when a strip of metallic Zinc ($\text{Zn}$) is immersed in an aqueous Copper(II) Sulfate solution ($\text{CuSO}_4$)?

options.A: Zinc dissolves into colorless $\text{Zn}^{2+}$ ions, blue color fades, and reddish-brown Copper metal precipitates on the strip
options.B: No reaction occurs because copper is more active than zinc
options.C: Vigorous evolution of toxic chlorine gas occurs
options.D: The solution turns bright yellow with no metal deposition

Electrochemistry.explanation: $\text{Zn}(s) + \text{Cu}^{2+}(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn}^{2+}(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)$. Zinc is higher in the activity series, so it readily reduces copper ions to metallic copper.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: According to Faraday's First Law of Electrolysis, the mass ($m$) of a chemical substance liberated or deposited at an electrode during electrolysis is directly proportional to:

options.A: The total quantity of electrical charge ($Q = I \times t$) passed through the electrolyte ($m = ZIt$)
options.B: The total volume of the glass electrolytic tank
options.D: The color intensity of the electrolyte solution

Electrochemistry.explanation: Faraday's first law states $m \propto Q$, or $m = Z \cdot I \cdot t$, where $Z$ is the electrochemical equivalent, $I$ is current in amperes, and $t$ is time in seconds.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In the industrial electrolysis of aqueous brine ($\text{NaCl}(aq)$) using a Nelson's Diaphragm Cell, the three valuable commercial products formed are:

options.A: Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$), Chlorine gas ($\text{Cl}_2$), and Hydrogen gas ($\text{H}_2$)
options.B: Sodium metal, Oxygen gas, and Water
options.C: Hydrochloric acid, Sodium carbonate, and Ozone
options.D: Bleaching powder, Nitrogen gas, and Carbon monoxide

Electrochemistry.explanation: $2\text{NaCl} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\text{electrolysis}} 2\text{NaOH}(aq) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\uparrow + \text{H}_2(g)\uparrow$. Nelson's cell produces caustic soda, chlorine, and hydrogen.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.topic: Salt Bridge Function in Daniell Cell
Electrochemistry.question: What is the primary operational function of the Salt Bridge (containing $\text{KCl}$ in agar gel) in a galvanic Daniell Cell?

options.A: To maintain electrical neutrality in both half-cells by migrating ions and completing the internal electrical circuit
options.B: To speed up the flow of electrons through the external copper wire
options.C: To supply external voltage to the cell
options.D: To prevent zinc metal from dissolving

Electrochemistry.explanation: A salt bridge allows anions and cations to migrate between half-cells, preventing build-up of positive/negative charges and maintaining electrical neutrality without mixing solutions.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Which of the following aqueous solutions is classified as a Weak Electrolyte that ionizes only partially in water?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Acetic acid is a weak electrolyte with low degree of ionization ($\sim 1-2\%$ in water), conducting electricity weakly compared to strong acids like $\text{HCl}$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In the electroplating of a steel spoon with pure Silver ($\text{Ag}$), the steel spoon must be connected as:

options.A: The Cathode (negative terminal), immersed in aqueous Silver Potassium Cyanide ($\text{K[Ag(CN)}_2]$) electrolyte

Electrochemistry.explanation: In electroplating, the article to be coated is always made the cathode (negative electrode) where silver cations undergo reduction: $\text{Ag}^+ + e^- \rightarrow \text{Ag}(s)$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: By international convention, the Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE) is assigned an arbitrary standard reduction potential ($E^\circ$) of:
Electrochemistry.explanation: The SHE reaction: $2\text{H}^+(aq, 1\text{M}) + 2e^- \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_2(g, 1\text{atm})$ is defined as the universal reference standard with $E^circ = 0.00\text{ V}$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Faraday's Second Law of Electrolysis states that when the same quantity of electric charge passes through different electrolytes connected in series, the masses of substances liberated are directly proportional to their:

options.D: Surface area of the glass cell

Electrochemistry.explanation: Faraday's 2nd Law states $W_1 / W_2 = E_1 / E_2$, meaning the mass of an element discharged is proportional to its equivalent weight ($E = M/z$).

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Why are blocks of active Magnesium or Zinc attached to the underground steel pipelines and steel hulls of marine ships?

options.A: To serve as Sacrificial Anodes that oxidize preferentially because they have more negative reduction potentials, protecting iron from corrosion
options.B: To make the ship heavier in deep water
options.C: To conduct lightning strikes into the sea

Electrochemistry.explanation: Magnesium ($E^\circ = -2.37\text{ V}$) and Zinc ($E^\circ = -0.76\text{ V}$) oxidize more readily than Iron ($E^\circ = -0.44\text{ V}$), sacrificing themselves to keep iron cathodically protected.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: In a Hydrogen-Oxygen Fuel Cell generating clean electrical power in space vehicles, what is the sole chemical byproduct produced at the cathode?
Electrochemistry.explanation: Overall cell reaction: $2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{Electrical Energy}$. The only exhaust byproduct is pure water.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: The Standard Hydrogen Electrode (SHE), comprising a platinized platinum foil immersed in $1.0\text{ M } \text{H}^+$ solution bubbled with $\text{H}_2$ gas at $1\text{ atm}$ and $25^\circ\text{C}$, is assigned an arbitrary reference potential of:
Electrochemistry.explanation: SHE is the universal zero reference standard against which all other standard reduction electrode potentials ($E^circ$) are measured at $298\ext{ K}$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: During the electrolytic refining of impure copper, what is used as the Anode and what occurs to it during electrolysis?

options.A: Anode is impure blister copper, which oxidizes and dissolves into $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions, leaving valuable anode mud (gold, silver) at the bottom
options.B: Anode is pure copper where copper deposits
options.C: Anode is graphite that releases oxygen gas
options.D: Anode is solid iron that rusts

Electrochemistry.explanation: Impure copper acts as the anode ($\ext{Cu} \ightarrow \ext{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^-$), while pure copper sheets act as cathode ($\ext{Cu}^{2+} + 2e^- \ightarrow \ext{Cu}$). Precious impurities fall as anode mud.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: During the discharging of a rechargeable lead-acid car storage battery, both the lead anode ($\text{Pb}$) and lead dioxide cathode ($\text{PbO}_2$) are converted into:

options.A: Lead(II) Sulfate ($\text{PbSO}_4(s)$), diluting the sulfuric acid electrolyte

Electrochemistry.explanation: Discharging reaction: $\text{Pb}(s) + \text{PbO}_2(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{PbSO}_4(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, consuming acid and depositing white $\text{PbSO}_4$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: A redox electrochemical reaction is thermodynamically spontaneous under standard conditions if and only if its standard cell potential ($\Delta E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$) is:
Electrochemistry.explanation: Spontaneity relates to Gibbs free energy: $\Delta G^\circ = -nFE^\circ_{\text{cell}}$. A positive $E^\circ_{\text{cell}}$ produces a negative $\Delta G^\circ$, driving spontaneous current.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.topic: Electrolysis of Molten Lead Bromide Products
Electrochemistry.question: When molten Lead(II) Bromide ($\text{PbBr}_2(l)$) is electrolyzed using inert graphite electrodes, the products formed at the cathode and anode are respectively:

options.A: Silvery molten Lead metal at cathode, reddish-brown Bromine vapor at anode
options.B: Hydrogen gas at cathode, oxygen gas at anode
options.C: Bromine liquid at cathode, lead metal at anode
options.D: Lead oxide at cathode, graphite at anode

Electrochemistry.explanation: Cathode (reduction): $\text{Pb}^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow \text{Pb}(l)$; Anode (oxidation): $2\text{Br}^- \rightarrow \text{Br}_2(g) + 2e^-$.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.question: Modern rechargeable Lithium-ion batteries used in smartphones operate on the principle of Intercalation, which means:

options.A: Lithium ions ($\text{Li}^+$) reversibly insert and de-insert between crystal layers of graphite and transition metal oxides without metallic lithium plating
options.B: Lithium burns in air to generate heat
options.C: Water is decomposed into hydrogen gas

Electrochemistry.explanation: Intercalation involves reversible insertion of guest $\text{Li}^+$ ions into layered host lattices (graphite anode and $\text{LiCoO}_2$ cathode) during charge-discharge cycles.

Electrochemistry.subject: Chemistry
Electrochemistry.topic: Galvanizing vs Tin Plating for Food Cans
Electrochemistry.question: Why are food cans plated with Tin ($\text{Sn}$) rather than Zinc ($\text{Zn}$), even though Zinc provides superior sacrificial protection?

options.A: Tin is non-toxic and unreactive with organic food acids, whereas dissolved Zinc salts are poisonous
options.B: Zinc is too expensive to manufacture
options.D: Zinc dissolves into air within seconds

Electrochemistry.explanation: Zinc reacts with food organic acids (citric, acetic acid) to form toxic zinc salts. Tin is non-toxic and forms a protective inert oxide layer safe for food contact.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: A chemical reaction that absorbs thermal energy from its surroundings, causing the temperature of the reaction mixture to fall, is classified as:
Energetics.explanation: Endothermic reactions absorb heat from the surroundings (positive enthalpy change, $\Delta H > 0$), resulting in a decrease in surrounding temperature.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: In an Exothermic reaction, the enthalpy of products ($H_p$) compared to the enthalpy of reactants ($H_r$) is:

options.A: Less than reactants ($H_p < H_r$, so $\Delta H$ is negative)
options.B: Greater than reactants ($H_p > H_r$, so $\Delta H$ is positive)

Energetics.explanation: $\Delta H = H_p - H_r$. Since energy is released to surroundings in exothermic reactions, products have lower chemical enthalpy than reactants ($\Delta H$ is negative).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: The minimum amount of energy required by colliding reactant molecules to overcome repulsive barriers and form an activated complex is the:
Energetics.explanation: Activation energy ($E_a$) is the energy threshold needed to initiate a chemical reaction by breaking reactant bonds to form the transition state.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: How does a positive catalyst increase the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed?

options.A: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with a lower Activation Energy ($E_a$)
options.B: It increases the overall enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) of the reaction
options.C: It heats the reaction mixture to higher temperatures
options.D: It changes the equilibrium position constant $K_c$

Energetics.explanation: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by offering an alternate reaction mechanism having lower activation energy, allowing a greater fraction of collisions to be effective.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: The standard enthalpy of neutralization for the reaction between a strong acid and a strong base (e.g., $\text{HCl} + \text{NaOH}$) is approximately constant at:
Energetics.explanation: The net reaction for any strong acid-strong base neutralization is $\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, releasing about $-57.3\text{ kJ/mol}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: During any chemical transformation, bond breaking in reactants and bond forming in products are respectively:
Energetics.explanation: Breaking chemical bonds requires input of energy (endothermic process), while forming new chemical bonds releases energy (exothermic process).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: When measuring enthalpy changes using a calorimeter, what formula calculates the heat absorbed or released ($q$) by a mass $m$ of water with specific heat capacity $c$ over a temperature change $\Delta T$?
Energetics.explanation: Heat transferred $q = m c \Delta T$, where $m$ is mass, $c$ is specific heat capacity ($4.184\text{ J/g}^\circ\text{C}$ for water), and $\Delta T$ is the temperature change.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: In an energy profile diagram for an endothermic reaction, the transition state (activated complex) is located:

options.A: At the highest peak of the energy barrier above both reactants and products
options.C: At the exact same level as the products
options.D: At the origin of the coordinate axis

Energetics.explanation: The activated complex represents the maximum potential energy configuration along the reaction coordinate.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: The standard enthalpy of combustion ($\Delta H_c^\circ$) is defined as the enthalpy change when $1\text{ mole}$ of a substance is:

options.A: Completely burned in excess oxygen under standard conditions
options.B: Dissolved in infinite volume of water
options.C: Decomposed into its constituent gaseous elements
options.D: Neutralized by one mole of strong acid

Energetics.explanation: Standard enthalpy of combustion is the heat released when 1 mole of a substance undergoes complete oxidation in excess oxygen at standard conditions ($298\text{ K}, 1\text{ atm}$).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: Biological cellular respiration and photosynthesis are energetic counterparts. Photosynthesis is:

options.A: An endothermic reaction driven by absorbed solar radiant energy
options.C: A nuclear fission process in chloroplasts

Energetics.explanation: Photosynthesis ($6\text{CO}_2 + 6\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{light} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6 + 6\text{O}_2$) absorbs photon energy and is endothermic, whereas respiration releases energy and is exothermic.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: In chemical thermodynamics, an Exothermic reaction that releases heat to its surrounding environment is characterized by a sign of $\Delta H$ that is:

options.A: Negative ($\Delta H < 0$), because the enthalpy of products is lower than the enthalpy of reactants

Energetics.explanation: $\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}$. In exothermic reactions, system energy decreases as heat is released, resulting in $\Delta H < 0$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.topic: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation
Energetics.question: Hess's Law of Constant Heat Summation states that:

options.A: The overall enthalpy change for a chemical reaction is independent of the pathway or number of steps taken between initial reactants and final products
options.B: Heat always flows from cold objects to hot objects without work
options.C: All chemical reactions have identical enthalpy changes at $100^\circ\text{C}$
options.D: Enthalpy changes can only be measured for gaseous combustion

Energetics.explanation: Because enthalpy ($H$) is a thermodynamic state function, total $\Delta H$ depends only on initial and final states: $\Delta H_{\text{direct}} = \sum \Delta H_{\text{intermediate steps}}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: When one mole of aqueous strong monoprotic acid ($\text{HCl}$) is completely neutralized by one mole of strong base ($\text{NaOH}$) at $25^\circ\text{C}$, the standard enthalpy of neutralization ($\Delta H_n^\circ$) is approximately:
Energetics.explanation: Strong acid-base neutralization represents the formation of water from its ions: $\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, releasing $-57.3\text{ kJ/mol}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: How does adding a positive catalyst affect the Activation Energy ($E_a$) and Enthalpy Change ($\Delta H$) of a chemical reaction?

options.A: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower $E_a$, while leaving the overall $\Delta H$ completely unchanged
options.C: It converts an endothermic reaction into an exothermic one

Energetics.explanation: A catalyst lowers the kinetic activation energy barrier ($E_a$), accelerating forward and reverse rates equally without altering initial/final thermodynamic enthalpies ($Delta H$).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: Bond breaking is always an Endothermic process ($\Delta H > 0$), while bond forming is always an:
Energetics.explanation: Overcoming interatomic forces to break bonds requires energy input (endothermic), whereas forming stable chemical bonds releases energy (exothermic).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: In a coffee-cup calorimeter, $100\text{ g}$ of water is heated, and its temperature rises by $5.0^\circ\text{C}$. How much heat energy ($q$) was absorbed by the water? (Specific heat capacity of water $c = 4.184\text{ J/g}^\circ\text{C}$)
Energetics.explanation: $q = m \cdot c \cdot \Delta T = 100\text{ g} \times 4.184\text{ J/g}^\circ\text{C} \times 5.0^\circ\text{C} = 2092\text{ J} = 2.092\text{ kJ}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: In thermochemistry, standard thermodynamic states ($\Delta H^\circ$) are defined at which standard conditions?

options.A: $25^\circ\text{C}$ ($298.15\text{ K}$), $1\text{ atm}$ ($101.3\text{ kPa}$), and $1\text{ M}$ concentration for aqueous solutions

Energetics.explanation: Standard thermodynamic conditions specify temperature of $298.15\text{ K}$ ($25^\circ\text{C}$), pressure of $1\text{ bar}$ or $1\text{ atm}$, and concentration of $1.0\text{ mol/dm}^3$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: When Ammonium Nitrate ($\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$) dissolves in water inside an instant cold pack, the container feels cold to the touch because the dissolution process is:

options.A: Endothermic ($\Delta H > 0$), absorbing heat from the immediate surroundings

Energetics.explanation: The lattice energy of $\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$ exceeds its hydration energy, making the overall enthalpy of solution positive (endothermic), lowering the ambient temperature.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.topic: Standard Enthalpy of Formation for Pure Elements
Energetics.question: By thermodynamic convention, what is the Standard Enthalpy of Formation ($\Delta H_f^\circ$) for any pure element in its most stable standard physical state (e.g., $\text{O}_2(g), \text{C}(s, \text{graphite})$)?
Energetics.explanation: The standard enthalpy of formation of an element in its standard reference state (e.g., $\text{O}_2(g), \text{N}_2(g), \text{Fe}(s), \text{C}(\text{graphite})$) is defined as zero.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: A Bomb Calorimeter is an insulated, constant-volume thermodynamic device specially designed to accurately measure:

options.A: Standard Enthalpy of Combustion ($\Delta H_c^\circ$) of fuels and organic foodstuffs
options.C: The speed of sound in air

Energetics.explanation: A bomb calorimeter ignites a sample in pressurized oxygen at constant volume, measuring the heat evolved to determine standard enthalpies of combustion ($Delta H_c^circ$).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: Calculate the thermal heat absorbed ($q$) when $200.0\text{ g}$ of water is heated from $20.0^\circ\text{C}$ to $50.0^\circ\text{C}$. (Specific heat capacity of water $c = 4.184\text{ J}/(\text{g}\cdot^\circ\text{C})$)
Energetics.explanation: $q = mc\Delta T = 200.0\text{ g} \times 4.184\text{ J}/(\text{g}\cdot^\circ\text{C}) \times (50.0 - 20.0^\circ\text{C}) = 200 \times 4.184 \times 30 = 25,104\text{ J} = 25.10\text{ kJ}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: For the reaction $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)$, given bond energies: $\text{H}-\text{H} = 436\text{ kJ/mol}, \text{Cl}-\text{Cl} = 242\text{ kJ/mol}, \text{H}-\text{Cl} = 431\text{ kJ/mol}$, what is the Enthalpy of Reaction ($\Delta H$)?
Energetics.explanation: $\Delta H = \sum D(\text{bonds broken}) - \sum D(\text{bonds formed}) = [436 + 242] - [2 \times 431] = 678 - 862 = -184\text{ kJ/mol}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: The Standard Enthalpy of Formation ($\Delta H_f^\circ$) of any pure chemical element in its most stable standard thermodynamic physical state at $298\text{ K}$ and $1\text{ atm}$ (e.g., $\text{O}_2(g), \text{C}(\text{graphite}), \text{Fe}(s)$) is defined as:
Energetics.explanation: By thermodynamic convention, $\Delta H_f^\circ = 0$ for all pure chemical elements in their standard reference states (e.g., $\text{O}_2(g), \text{N}_2(g), \text{C}(\text{graphite})$).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.topic: First Law of Thermodynamics (Conservation of Energy)
Energetics.question: The First Law of Thermodynamics, mathematically expressed as $\Delta U = q + w$, establishes that:

options.A: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; the total energy of the universe remains constant
options.B: Entropy of the universe always decreases to zero
options.C: Heat always flows from cold to hot spontaneously
options.D: Matter turns into energy at absolute zero

Energetics.explanation: The 1st Law states conservation of energy: change in internal energy $\Delta U$ equals heat added $q$ plus work done on the system $w$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: Which of the following thermodynamic quantities is a true State Function whose change depends solely on initial and final states, not the path taken?
Energetics.explanation: State functions ($P, V, T, U, H, S, G$) depend only on the thermodynamic state of the system, whereas heat ($q$) and work ($w$) are path-dependent functions.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: A steel Bomb Calorimeter is specifically designed to measure the heat of combustion of fuels and foods at:

options.A: Constant Volume ($\Delta V = 0$, measuring change in internal energy $\Delta U = q_v$)
options.B: Constant atmospheric pressure open to air

Energetics.explanation: A rigid sealed bomb calorimeter maintains constant volume ($w = -P\Delta V = 0$), so the measured heat of combustion directly equals internal energy change $\Delta U$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: Commercial instant emergency cold packs become ice-cold within seconds of squeezing because of the highly endothermic dissolution of:

options.A: Ammonium Nitrate ($\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3$) in water ($\Delta H_{\text{soln}} = +25.7\text{ kJ/mol}$)

Energetics.explanation: Dissolving ammonium nitrate absorbs substantial lattice hydration thermal energy from surroundings ($Delta H > 0$), dropping temperature near $0^circ\ext{C}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: When a chemical catalyst is added to an exothermic reaction, how does it alter the reaction's Potential Energy Profile diagram?

options.A: It provides an alternative reaction pathway with lower Activation Energy ($E_a$), while overall enthalpy change ($\Delta H$) remains unchanged
options.B: It makes $\Delta H$ much more negative
options.D: It increases activation energy to prevent side reactions

Energetics.explanation: Catalysts lower the activation energy barrier ($E_a$) for both forward and reverse reactions without altering initial reactant or final product energy states ($\Delta H$ is constant).

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.question: The standard enthalpy of neutralization for any strong monoprotic acid reacting with any strong base in dilute aqueous solution ($\text{H}^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}$) has a constant value of approximately:
Energetics.explanation: Strong acids and bases completely dissociate in water. The net reaction is purely $\text{H}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, releasing a constant $-57.3\text{ kJ/mol}$.

Energetics.subject: Chemistry
Energetics.topic: Spontaneity and Gibbs Free Energy Equation
Energetics.question: The Gibbs Free Energy equation ($\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$) dictates that a chemical reaction is unconditionally spontaneous at all temperatures when:

options.A: Enthalpy change is negative ($\Delta H < 0$, exothermic) and Entropy change is positive ($\Delta S > 0$)

Energetics.explanation: When $\Delta H < 0$ and $\Delta S > 0$, the term $\Delta G = \Delta H - T\Delta S$ is always negative ($Delta G < 0$) regardless of temperature $T$, ensuring spontaneous reaction.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: In a closed chemical system at Dynamic Chemical Equilibrium, what is true regarding the forward and reverse reaction rates?

options.A: The rate of the forward reaction equals the rate of the reverse reaction
options.B: All forward and reverse reactions cease completely
options.C: The concentration of products must exactly equal the concentration of reactants
options.D: The forward reaction proceeds at twice the speed of the reverse reaction

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium is reached when forward and backward reaction rates become equal, keeping macroscopic concentrations constant while microscopic reactions continue.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the reversible gas-phase reaction: $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$, what is the correct equilibrium constant expression ($K_c$)?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: By the Law of Mass Action, $K_c$ is the ratio of product concentrations raised to their stoichiometric coefficients over reactant concentrations raised to theirs.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If a reversible chemical reaction has an exceptionally large equilibrium constant value (e.g., $K_c = 10^{15}$), this indicates that:

options.A: The reaction proceeds almost to completion and products predominate at equilibrium
options.B: Reactants are overwhelmingly favored and very little product forms
options.C: The reaction cannot take place under any conditions
options.D: The reaction rate is infinitely slow

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: A very large $K_c$ ($K_c \gg 1$) indicates that at equilibrium the numerator (products) is vastly larger than the denominator (reactants), meaning near-complete forward conversion.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, what happens to the equilibrium position if additional reactant is continuously added to a system at equilibrium?

options.A: The equilibrium shifts to the right (forward direction) to consume the added reactant
options.B: The equilibrium shifts to the left to produce more reactant
options.D: The total pressure drops to zero

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Le Chatelier's principle states that if a system at equilibrium is disturbed, it adjusts to counteract the disturbance; adding reactant shifts the reaction forward.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the equilibrium $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$ ($4\text{ moles of gas} \rightarrow 2\text{ moles of gas}$), increasing the total external pressure will:

options.A: Shift the equilibrium towards the right (forward direction) producing more Ammonia
options.B: Shift the equilibrium towards the left producing more Nitrogen
options.C: Have no effect on the equilibrium position
options.D: Cause the value of $K_c$ to double

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Increasing pressure favors the direction that produces fewer moles of gas (2 moles of $\text{NH}_3$ vs 4 moles of reactants), shifting the system to the right.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For an Exothermic equilibrium reaction ($\Delta H < 0$), increasing the temperature of the system will:

options.A: Shift the equilibrium in the backward (endothermic) direction and decrease $K_c$
options.B: Shift the equilibrium forward and increase $K_c$
options.C: Have no impact on the concentrations

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: In an exothermic reaction, heat is a product. Adding heat shifts the equilibrium in the reverse endothermic direction to absorb excess thermal energy, decreasing $K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: What effect does adding a catalyst have on the equilibrium position and the value of $K_c$ in a reversible reaction?

options.A: It speeds up both forward and reverse reactions equally, reaching equilibrium faster without changing $K_c$
options.B: It shifts the equilibrium forward and increases $K_c$
options.C: It shifts the equilibrium backward and decreases $K_c$
options.D: It prevents equilibrium from ever being attained

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: A catalyst lowers the activation energy of both forward and reverse pathways by the same amount; it shortens the time to reach equilibrium without altering equilibrium concentrations or $K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: Which of the following chemical processes is classified as an Irreversible reaction that goes to completion in an open system?

options.B: Haber process for Ammonia synthesis in a closed reactor
options.C: Contact process for $\text{SO}_3$ formation in a closed tube
options.D: Dissociation of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ into $\text{NO}_2$ in a sealed flask

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Combustion reactions release high energy and gaseous products in an open atmosphere, proceeding unidirectionally to completion with no reverse reaction.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: What are the units of $K_c$ for the decomposition reaction: $\text{PCl}_5(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)$?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: $K_c = \frac{[\text{PCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{PCl}_5]} = \frac{(\text{mol/dm}^3)(\text{mol/dm}^3)}{\text{mol/dm}^3} = \text{mol} \cdot \text{dm}^{-3}$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: The Law of Mass Action, which relates reaction rate to active masses of reactants, was formulated by:

options.C: Svante Arrhenius and J.H. van 't Hoff

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Norwegian chemists Cato Maximilian Guldberg and Peter Waage proposed the Law of Mass Action in 1864.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: Formulated in 1864 by Guldberg and Waage, the Law of Mass Action states that the rate of a chemical reaction at any instant is directly proportional to:

options.A: The product of the active masses (molar concentrations) of the reacting substances raised to powers of their stoichiometric coefficients
options.B: The total volume of the reaction vessel
options.C: The total mass of the catalyst
options.D: The surface tension of the solvent

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: The law of mass action states: $\text{Rate} \propto [A]^a [B]^b$, where $[A]$ and $[B]$ represent active molar concentrations.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Equilibrium Constant Expression for Ammonia Synthesis
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the Haber equilibrium reaction: $\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)$, what is the correct mathematical expression for the equilibrium constant ($K_c$)?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Products are placed in the numerator and reactants in the denominator, each raised to their stoichiometric powers: $K_c = [\text{NH}_3]^2 / ([\text{N}_2][\text{H}_2]^3)$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the equilibrium system: $2\text{SO}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3(g)$ ($3\text{ moles of gas} \rightarrow 2\text{ moles of gas}$), how will increasing the total external pressure shift the equilibrium?

options.A: Shifts to the right (forward direction), toward the side with fewer gas moles ($2\text{ moles of } \text{SO}_3$)
options.C: Has zero effect on equilibrium composition

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: According to Le Chatelier's Principle, increasing pressure shifts the equilibrium in the direction that decreases the total number of gas molecules ($3\text{ mol} \rightarrow 2\text{ mol}$, forward).

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Reaction Quotient (Qc) vs Kc Direction Prediction
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If at a specific point in a reversible reaction the calculated Reaction Quotient is smaller than the Equilibrium Constant ($Q_c < K_c$), how will the system respond to reach equilibrium?

options.A: The reaction will proceed in the forward direction (generating more products) until $Q_c = K_c$
options.B: The reaction will proceed in the reverse direction
options.C: The system is already at dynamic equilibrium
options.D: The value of $K_c$ will decrease to match $Q_c$

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: When $Q_c < K_c$, there are fewer products relative to reactants than at equilibrium; the reaction shifts forward to produce more products until $Q_c = K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: In the heterogeneous thermal decomposition equilibrium of limestone: $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$, why are solid $\text{CaCO}_3$ and $\text{CaO}$ omitted from the $K_c$ expression?

options.A: The molar concentration (density) of pure solids remains constant and is incorporated into the equilibrium constant ($K_c = [\text{CO}_2]$)
options.B: Solids do not contain chemical bonds
options.C: Carbon dioxide is the only reactant present

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: The active mass/concentration of a pure solid depends solely on its density and molar mass, remaining constant during reaction. Thus, $K_c = [\text{CO}_2]$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: What are the derived units of $K_c$ for the equilibrium reaction: $\text{H}_2(g) + \text{I}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{HI}(g)$?

options.A: No units (dimensionless), because the sum of reactant coefficients equals the sum of product coefficients ($\Delta n = 2 - 2 = 0$)

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Units of $K_c = (\text{mol/dm}^3)^{\Delta n}$. Here $\Delta n = 2 - (1+1) = 0$; $(\text{mol/dm}^3)^0 = 1$ (no units).

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Effect of Catalyst on Equilibrium Position
Chemical Equilibrium.question: What is the exact effect of adding a finely divided Iron catalyst to the Haber Ammonia equilibrium system?

options.A: It increases the rates of both forward and reverse reactions equally, reaching equilibrium faster without changing the equilibrium yield or $K_c$
options.B: It increases the net percentage yield of ammonia by $50\%$
options.C: It shifts the equilibrium completely to the reactants side
options.D: It doubles the numerical value of $K_c$

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: A catalyst speeds up attainment of equilibrium by lowering activation energy for both directions equally; it does NOT alter the equilibrium concentrations, yield, or $K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If a reversible chemical reaction has an extremely small equilibrium constant ($K_c = 10^{-15}$), this indicates that at equilibrium:

options.A: Reactants are overwhelmingly favored and only negligible trace amounts of products are formed
options.B: The reaction goes virtually to $100\%$ completion

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: A very small $K_c \ll 1$ signifies that very little product is present at equilibrium, indicating the forward reaction occurs to a negligible extent.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Le Chatelier's Principle - Temperature Effect on Endothermic System
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For an endothermic reversible reaction ($\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) + \text{Heat} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g), \Delta H > 0$), what will be observed when the reaction vessel is heated?

options.A: The equilibrium shifts forward, increasing the concentration of dark reddish-brown $\text{NO}_2$ gas and increasing $K_c$
options.B: The equilibrium shifts reverse, making the mixture colorless
options.C: The total pressure drops to zero

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: For an endothermic reaction, heat acts as a reactant. Supplying heat shifts the equilibrium forward to absorb excess thermal energy, producing more brown $\text{NO}_2$ and increasing $K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: Why is chemical equilibrium termed 'Dynamic' rather than 'Static'?

options.A: Forward and reverse chemical reactions continue to occur simultaneously at identical microscopic rates ($r_f = r_r$)
options.B: All molecular motion halts completely at equilibrium
options.C: The reaction vessel continuously moves across the laboratory
options.D: Reactants are continuously destroyed into energy

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Dynamic equilibrium is an active balance where opposing forward and reverse processes continue at equal rates, keeping macroscopic concentrations invariant.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Equilibrium Constant Expression for Heterogeneous Equilibria
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the heterogeneous thermal decomposition equilibrium $\text{CaCO}_3(s) \rightleftharpoons \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)$, what is the correct equilibrium constant expression ($K_c$)?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: In heterogeneous equilibria, the concentrations of pure solid phases ($\ext{CaCO}_3, \ext{CaO}$) are constant and incorporated into the equilibrium constant: $K_c = [\ext{CO}_2]$ (or $K_p = P_{\ext{CO}_2}$).

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If at a particular moment in a reacting mixture the Reaction Quotient ($Q_c$) is less than the Equilibrium Constant ($Q_c < K_c$), the system will:

options.A: Shift in the forward direction (left to right) to convert more reactants into products until $Q_c = K_c$

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: When $Q_c < K_c$, product concentrations are lower than required for equilibrium. The reaction proceeds forward to increase products until $Q_c = K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: In the industrial synthesis of Ammonia ($\text{N}_2 + 3\text{H}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3, \Delta H = -92\text{ kJ/mol}$), why is an optimum compromise temperature of $450^\circ\text{C}$ used rather than room temperature?

options.A: To achieve an economically viable reaction rate while maintaining an acceptable equilibrium yield in the presence of an Iron catalyst
options.B: Because the reaction is impossible below $400^\circ\text{C}$
options.C: To prevent iron catalyst from turning into gold
options.D: To freeze the ammonia into solid blocks

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Although lower temperature thermodynamically favors exothermic ammonia yield, the kinetic rate is too slow. $450^\circ\text{C}$ with iron catalyst balances rate and yield.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Effect of Adding an Inert Gas at Constant Volume
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If an inert noble gas (such as Argon) is pumped into an equilibrium system ($2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3$) at Constant Volume, what is the effect on the equilibrium position?

options.A: No effect on equilibrium position because partial pressures and molar concentrations of reacting gases remain unchanged

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Adding an inert gas at constant volume increases total pressure, but does not alter partial pressures or concentrations of reactants/products; hence equilibrium position is unaffected.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Contact Process for Sulfuric Acid Catalyst
Chemical Equilibrium.question: In the Contact Process, the catalytic oxidation of sulfur dioxide ($2\text{SO}_2 + \text{O}_2 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{SO}_3$) uses which industrial catalyst at $450^\circ\text{C}$?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Vanadium pentoxide ($\ext{V}_2\ext{O}_5$) provides an active surface at $450^circ\ext{C}$ to catalyze the conversion of $\ext{SO}_2$ to $\ext{SO}_3$ in the manufacture of sulfuric acid.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Equilibrium Constant Units for Equal Moles
Chemical Equilibrium.question: For the esterification equilibrium $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} + \text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{CH}_3\text{COOC}_2\text{H}_5 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, what are the units of $K_c$?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: When total moles of gaseous/aqueous products equal total moles of reactants ($\Delta n = 0$), concentration units cancel out completely, making $K_c$ dimensionless.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Magnitude of Kc and Extent of Reaction
Chemical Equilibrium.question: If a reversible chemical reaction has an extremely large equilibrium constant ($K_c = 10^{20}$), this quantitatively indicates that:

options.A: The reaction proceeds almost to completion, with products vastly dominating at equilibrium
options.C: Reactants and products are present in exact 50:50 equal amounts

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: A very large $K_c \gg 1$ indicates that the numerator (products) is enormous compared to denominator (reactants), meaning the forward reaction goes virtually to completion.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: Why is chemical equilibrium classified as 'Dynamic' rather than 'Static'?

options.A: Forward and reverse reactions continue to occur simultaneously at exactly identical rates ($r_f = r_r$), so macroscopic concentrations remain constant
options.B: All chemical molecules freeze into rigid crystals
options.C: The reaction container rotates dynamically in space

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Chemical equilibrium is dynamic because molecular collisions and transformations never stop; microscopic forward and backward rates are equal, creating constant macroscopic state.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.question: According to van 't Hoff's relationship, for an Endothermic reaction ($\Delta H > 0$), what happens to the value of $K_c$ when the temperature is raised?
Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: In endothermic reactions, heat acts like a reactant. Increasing temperature shifts equilibrium forward to absorb heat, increasing product concentrations and raising $K_c$.

Chemical Equilibrium.subject: Chemistry
Chemical Equilibrium.topic: Le Chatelier's Principle - N2O4 and NO2 Equilibrium
Chemical Equilibrium.question: In the gaseous equilibrium $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\text{ (colorless)} \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2\text{ (brown)}, \Delta H = +57\text{ kJ/mol}$, placing the sealed tube in an ice bath will:

options.A: Turn the mixture lighter / colorless as equilibrium shifts to the exothermic reverse direction forming $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$
options.B: Turn the mixture intensely dark brown
options.C: Cause the glass tube to explode from pressure

Chemical Equilibrium.explanation: Cooling an endothermic forward reaction shifts equilibrium in the reverse exothermic direction according to Le Chatelier's principle, forming colorless $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: According to Svante Arrhenius's theory of acids and bases, a Base is defined as any substance that:

options.A: Dissociates in aqueous solution to yield Hydroxide ions ($\text{OH}^-$)
options.B: Dissociates in aqueous solution to produce Hydrogen ions ($\text{H}^+$)
options.C: Donates a proton to another chemical species
options.D: Accepts a lone pair of electrons

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: According to Arrhenius, an acid generates $\text{H}^+$ ions in water, whereas a base generates $\text{OH}^-$ ions.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: According to the Bronsted-Lowry acid-base theory, water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) can donate a proton as well as accept a proton, behaving as an:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Water behaves as an amphoteric compound because it acts as a base with acids (accepting a proton to form $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) and as an acid with bases (donating a proton to form $\text{OH}^-$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: In pure water or any neutral aqueous solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$, the sum of $pH$ and $pOH$ is always:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: At $25^\circ\text{C}$, the autoionization constant of water $K_w = [H^+][OH^-] = 10^{-14}$. Taking negative logarithms yields $pH + pOH = 14$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: What is the characteristic color of Phenolphthalein indicator in an acidic solution and in a strongly basic solution, respectively?

options.A: Colorless in acid, Pink / Magenta in base
options.B: Pink in acid, Colorless in base
options.C: Red in acid, Blue in base
options.D: Yellow in acid, Green in base

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral solutions ($pH < 8.2$) and turns distinct pink/magenta in alkaline solutions ($pH > 8.2$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Which of the following salts is classified as an Acidic Salt formed by partial neutralization of a diprotic acid?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{NaHCO}_3$ contains a replaceable hydrogen atom derived from partial neutralization of carbonic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$), making it an acid salt.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: When dilute Hydrochloric Acid reacts with solid Calcium Carbonate (marble chips), which gas is evolved with vigorous effervescence?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{CaCO}_3 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{CaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$. Acids react with metal carbonates to evolve carbon dioxide gas.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Which metallic oxide exhibits Amphoteric behavior, reacting with both strong acids and strong bases to form salt and water?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{Al}_2\text{O}_3$ and $\text{ZnO}$ are amphoteric oxides that neutralize both acids (acting as a basic oxide) and alkalis (acting as an acidic oxide).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$, found in vinegar) is classified as a Weak Acid because:

options.A: It ionizes only partially (incompletely) in aqueous solution
options.B: It does not contain any hydrogen atoms
options.C: It has a bitter taste and turns red litmus blue
options.D: It reacts violently with glass containers

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: A weak acid ionizes only slightly in water, establishing an equilibrium between undissociated molecules and ions ($< 5\%$ dissociation).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Plaster of Paris, widely used in orthopedics to set fractured bones and in statue molding, has the chemical formula:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Heating gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to $100^\circ\text{C}$ forms Plaster of Paris: $\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: In the Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction: $\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$, what is the conjugate acid of the base $\text{NH}_3$?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: A conjugate acid is formed when a Bronsted base accepts a proton ($\text{H}^+$). Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) gains $\text{H}^+$ to become $\text{NH}_4^+$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.topic: Lewis Concept of Acids and Bases
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: According to the Lewis electronic definition, a Lewis Acid is any chemical species that acts as an:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: G.N. Lewis defined an acid as an electron-pair acceptor (possessing vacant orbitals) and a base as an electron-pair donor.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: According to the Bronsted-Lowry theory, what is the Conjugate Base of Sulfuric Acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$)?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: A conjugate base is formed when an acid loses a single proton ($\text{H}^+$). Removing $\text{H}^+$ from $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ yields $\text{HSO}_4^-$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.topic: pOH and pH Relationship in Pure Water
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: In any aqueous solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$, the mathematical relationship between $pH$ and $pOH$ is governed by:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Autoionization of water gives $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$. Taking negative logarithms: $pH + pOH = 14.0$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: In an acid-base titration, Phenolphthalein indicator displays which distinct colors in acidic solution ($pH < 8.2$) and alkaline solution ($pH > 10$) respectively?

options.A: Colorless in acidic solution, and Pink / Magenta in alkaline solution
options.B: Bright yellow in acidic, and Deep blue in alkaline
options.C: Red in acidic, and Green in alkaline
options.D: Orange in acidic, and Violet in alkaline

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic and neutral media ($pH < 8.2$) and turns vibrant pink/magenta in basic solutions ($pH > 8.2-10.0$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: A Buffer Solution (e.g., a mixture of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) is chemically characterized by its ability to:

options.A: Resist drastic changes in $pH$ upon the addition of small amounts of strong acid or strong base
options.B: Change into concentrated sulfuric acid spontaneously

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: A buffer consists of a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid) that neutralizes added $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$, stabilizing $pH$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Potash Alum ($\text{K}_2\text{SO}_4 \cdot \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3 \cdot 24\text{H}_2\text{O}$) and Mohr's Salt ($\text{FeSO}_4 \cdot (\text{NH}_4)_2\text{SO}_4 \cdot 6\text{H}_2\text{O}$) are classic examples of:

options.A: Double Salts (equimolar combinations of two simple salts that retain individual ionic identities in solution)
options.B: Complex coordination salts with inert ligands

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Double salts crystallize from equimolar mixtures of two distinct simple salts and completely dissociate into their separate constituent ions when dissolved in water.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: When Sodium Carbonate ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$, salt of weak acid $\text{H}_2\text{CO}_3$ and strong base $\text{NaOH}$) dissolves in water, the resulting solution is:

options.A: Basic / Alkaline ($pH > 7$), due to anion hydrolysis producing excess $\text{OH}^-$ ions

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Carbonate ions undergo hydrolysis: $\text{CO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HCO}_3^- + \text{OH}^-$, generating excess $\text{OH}^-$ ions and yielding an alkaline solution ($pH > 7$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: When dilute Hydrochloric Acid ($\text{HCl}$) is added to solid Sodium Hydrogen Carbonate ($\text{NaHCO}_3$, baking soda), the brisk effervescence observed is due to the evolution of:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{NaHCO}_3 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$. Acids decompose hydrogen carbonates to yield carbon dioxide gas.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.topic: Calculation of pH of Strong Base
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: What is the $pH$ of a $0.01\text{ M}$ ($10^{-2}\text{ M}$) aqueous solution of Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$)?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{NaOH}$ is a strong base: $[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-2}\text{ M} \Rightarrow pOH = -\log(10^{-2}) = 2.0$. $pH = 14.0 - pOH = 14.0 - 2.0 = 12.0$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.topic: Water of Crystallization in Washing Soda
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: What is the chemical formula of hydrated Washing Soda containing 10 molecules of water of crystallization?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Washing soda is sodium carbonate decahydrate ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 \cdot 10\text{H}_2\text{O}$), which effloresces in dry air to form sodium carbonate monohydrate.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: How does an Acidic Buffer solution (e.g., Equimolar mixture of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and $\text{CH}_3\text{COONa}$) resist changes in $pH$ upon adding a small amount of strong acid ($\text{H}^+$)?

options.A: Added $\text{H}^+$ ions are consumed by the conjugate base acetate ions: $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$
options.C: Sodium ions precipitate as metallic sodium
options.D: The solution turns into pure sulfuric acid

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: The high concentration of conjugate base ($\ext{CH}_3\ext{COO}^-$) reacts with added $\ext{H}^+$ to form weak undissociated acetic acid, preserving constant $[\ext{H}^+]$ and $pH$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: The autoionization of pure water ($2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{OH}^-$) has an ionic product constant ($K_w$) at $25^\circ\text{C}$ of:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $K_w = [\text{H}^+][\text{OH}^-] = (1.0 \times 10^{-7})(1.0 \times 10^{-7}) = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$, yielding $pH + pOH = 14$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: When Ammonia ($\text{NH}_3$) reacts with Boron Trifluoride ($\text{BF}_3$) to form $\text{H}_3\text{N}:\rightarrow\text{BF}_3$, which reactant is the Lewis Acid and why?

options.A: $\text{BF}_3$ is the Lewis Acid because its central boron has an incomplete octet and accepts an electron pair from the nitrogen atom
options.B: $\text{NH}_3$ is the Lewis Acid because it donates protons
options.D: Neither is an acid or base

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: By G.N. Lewis's definition, an acid is an electron pair acceptor ($\ext{BF}_3$, sextet on B) and a base is an electron pair donor ($\ext{NH}_3$, lone pair on N).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: An aqueous solution of Ammonium Chloride ($\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, salt of weak base $\text{NH}_4\text{OH}$ and strong acid $\text{HCl}$) is:

options.A: Slightly acidic ($pH < 7$) due to cationic hydrolysis of $\text{NH}_4^+$ releasing $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ ions

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Cationic hydrolysis: $\text{NH}_4^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. The excess hydronium ions make the solution acidic ($pH < 7$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.topic: Effervescence of Carbonate Salts with Acid
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: When dilute Nitric acid ($\text{HNO}_3$) is poured onto solid Sodium Carbonate ($\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$), vigorous effervescence occurs due to the rapid evolution of:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3 + 2\text{HNO}_3 \rightarrow 2\text{NaNO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2\uparrow$. Acids react with metal carbonates/bicarbonates to liberate $\text{CO}_2$.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Aluminum Hydroxide ($\text{Al(OH)}_3$) is described as Amphoteric because it:

options.A: Dissolves in both strong acids (forming $\text{Al}^{3+}$ salts) and strong bases (forming aluminate $[\text{Al(OH)}_4]^-$ complexes)

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Amphoteric substances react with both acids ($\ext{Al(OH)}_3 + 3\ext{HCl} \ightarrow \ext{AlCl}_3 + 3\ext{H}_2\ext{O}$) and bases ($\ext{Al(OH)}_3 + \ext{NaOH} \ightarrow \ext{Na}[ \ext{Al(OH)}_4]$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: What color does Universal Indicator solution turn when added to a strongly basic solution of Sodium Hydroxide ($pH \approx 13-14$)?
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Universal indicator displays a color spectrum: Red (strong acid, $pH\,1-3$), Green (neutral, $pH\,7$), Blue (weak base, $pH\,9-10$), and Violet/Purple (strong base, $pH\,13-14$).

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: What is the $pH$ of a $0.001\text{ M } (1.0 \times 10^{-3}\text{ M})$ solution of Sodium Hydroxide ($\text{NaOH}$) at $25^\circ\text{C}$?

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Which general method is used to prepare an insoluble salt like Barium Sulfate ($\text{BaSO}_4$)?

options.A: Double decomposition / Precipitation by mixing two aqueous soluble salt solutions (e.g., $\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4\downarrow + 2\text{NaCl}$)
options.B: Reacting a metal with hydrogen gas
options.C: Direct heating of barium metal in air

Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Insoluble salts are prepared by precipitation (ionic double replacement) mixing solutions of two soluble salts, filtering and washing the solid residue.

Acids, Bases, and Salts.subject: Chemistry
Acids, Bases, and Salts.question: Plaster of Paris ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}\text{H}_2\text{O}$), used for setting fractured bones and statues, is manufactured by heating Gypsum ($\text{CaSO}_4 \cdot 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to:
Acids, Bases, and Salts.explanation: Controlled heating of gypsum at 100-120°C removes 1.5 water molecules: CaSO4 . 2H2O -> CaSO4 . 0.5H2O + 1.5H2O at 100°C.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Which layer of Earth's atmosphere lies immediately above the troposphere and contains the protective Ozone Layer?
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: The stratosphere extends from about 12 to 50 km above Earth's surface and houses the ozone layer ($\text{O}_3$), which absorbs harmful solar UV-B radiation.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Atmospheric Sulfur Dioxide ($\text{SO}_2$) gas, a principal precursor to industrial smog and acid rain, is released predominantly by:

options.A: Combustion of sulfur-containing fossil fuels (coal and crude oil) in thermal power stations and smelting plants
options.D: Decomposition of sand and quartz minerals

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Coal and heavy petroleum contain elemental sulfur and pyrite ($1-4\%$); during combustion, sulfur oxidizes to toxic sulfur dioxide: $\text{S} + \text{O}_2 \rightarrow \text{SO}_2$.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Photochemical smog is formed on warm, sunny days through reactions between sunlight, volatile organic compounds (VOCs), and:
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Sunlight triggers photochemical reactions between vehicular $\text{NO}_x$ and unburned hydrocarbons, producing tropospheric ozone, PAN, and brownish haze.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: In the stratosphere, Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) release which reactive radical under UV radiation that catalytically decomposes ozone ($\text{O}_3$)?
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: UV light breaks $\text{C}-\text{Cl}$ bonds in CFCs, releasing $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ radicals. A single chlorine radical can destroy up to $100,000$ ozone molecules.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Which of the following atmospheric trace gases is the most potent greenhouse gas per molecule, possessing a Global Warming Potential thousands of times greater than $\text{CO}_2$?
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Fluorinated gases like $\text{SF}_6$ and CFCs have extremely high global warming potentials ($> 20,000$ times that of $\text{CO}_2$) and very long atmospheric lifetimes.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Acid rain typically has a $pH$ value lower than:
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Unpolluted rainwater has a natural $pH$ of around $5.6$ due to dissolved atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$ forming carbonic acid. Precipitation with $pH < 5.6$ is defined as acid rain.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Modern automobiles are equipped with three-way catalytic converters containing platinum/palladium/rhodium to convert toxic $\text{CO}$ and unburned hydrocarbons into:
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Catalytic converters oxidize toxic $\text{CO}$ to $\text{CO}_2$ and unburned hydrocarbons to $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, while reducing $\text{NO}_x$ to harmless $\text{N}_2$.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Fine Particulate Matter ($\text{PM}_{2.5}$) is considered especially dangerous to human health because:

options.A: Its microscopic aerodynamic diameter ($< 2.5\,\mu\text{m}$) allows it to penetrate deep into pulmonary alveoli and enter the bloodstream
options.B: It is composed entirely of radioactive uranium
options.C: It reacts instantly with skin to cause electrical shock

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Particles with diameter $< 2.5\,\mu\text{m}$ bypass upper respiratory mucosal defenses, entering deep lung alveoli and provoking cardiovascular and pulmonary disease.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: The chemical corrosion and yellowing of marble monuments (like the Taj Mahal) caused by acid rain is chemically known as 'Stone Cancer', resulting from the reaction of $\text{CaCO}_3$ with:

options.A: Sulfuric Acid ($\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) forming soluble Calcium Sulfate ($\text{CaSO}_4$)

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: $\text{CaCO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{CaSO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{CO}_2$. Acid rain leaches calcium carbonate out of architectural marble.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Which radioactive, noble noble gas is a major indoor air pollutant that seeps from radioactive decay of radium in underground soil and bedrock into basements?
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Radon gas ($^{222}\text{Rn}$) is an alpha-emitting noble gas product of uranium/radium decay that accumulates in unventilated basements, causing lung cancer.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.topic: Layers of the Atmosphere - Stratospheric Ozone
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: In which layer of Earth's atmosphere is the protective Ozone Layer ($\text{O}_3$) located, shielding terrestrial life from harmful solar ultraviolet-B (UV-B) radiation?
Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: The stratosphere contains roughly $90\%$ of atmospheric ozone, where UV photolysis of $\text{O}_2$ creates $\text{O}_3$, absorbing lethal shortwave UV radiation.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.topic: Mechanism of Ozone Depletion by CFCs
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Why do Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs, e.g., $\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2$) cause catastrophic catalytic destruction of stratospheric ozone?

options.A: Solar UV radiation cleaves CFCs to release free Chlorine radicals ($\text{Cl}^\bullet$), each capable of decomposing over 100,000 ozone molecules via catalytic cycles
options.C: CFCs combine with nitrogen to make solid crystals
options.D: CFCs neutralize all water vapor in clouds

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: UV-C light releases chlorine free radicals: $\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \text{CF}_2\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{Cl}^\bullet$. The radical $\text{Cl}^\bullet + \text{O}_3 \rightarrow \text{ClO}^\bullet + \text{O}_2$ regenerates $\text{Cl}^\bullet$ repeatedly.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Photochemical smog (Los Angeles type smog) forms on sunny days through the complex photochemical reaction between sunlight and:

options.A: Nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$) and unburnt volatile organic hydrocarbons (VOCs), producing Ozone and PAN
options.B: Pure water vapor and table salt

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Solar UV initiates reactions between vehicle exhaust $\text{NO}_x$ and VOCs, producing secondary pollutants including tropospheric ozone, aldehydes, and peroxyacetyl nitrate (PAN).

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Three-way catalytic converters installed in vehicle exhaust systems convert toxic carbon monoxide ($\text{CO}$), nitrogen oxides ($\text{NO}_x$), and unburnt hydrocarbons into:

options.A: Harmless Carbon Dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$), Nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$), and Water vapor ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$)

Environmental Chemistry – Air.explanation: Using Platinum, Palladium, and Rhodium catalysts, converters oxidize $\text{CO} \rightarrow \text{CO}_2$ and $\text{C}_x\text{H}_y \rightarrow \text{CO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, while reducing $\text{NO}_x \rightarrow \text{N}_2$.

Environmental Chemistry – Air.subject: Chemistry
Environmental Chemistry – Air.question: Natural unpolluted rainwater is slightly acidic ($pH \approx 5.6$) due to dissolved atmospheric $\text{CO}_2$. Precipitation is officially defined as Acid Rain when its $pH$ falls below:
